summaries.title: Composition versus Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition are two competing ways neural networks encode features, trading off representational power against interpretability.

summaries.title: Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition
summaries.gist: Neurons can encode shapes and colors through four coding schemes ranging from local to compositional to fully superposed, each with different tradeoffs.
summaries.question: distributed representations — what different coding schemes reveal about composition and superposition? (four examples)

summaries.title: Two Notions of Distributed Representations
summaries.gist: "Distributed representations" combine two distinct ideas, composition and superposition, illustrated using Thorpe's four example neural codes for encoding colored shapes, which trade off differently in generalization and interpretability.

summaries.title: "Local" Codes
summaries.gist: A local code gives each shape-color pair its own neuron, wasting neurons but letting any combination be linearly selected, though a probe finding "red" need not mean a true red feature exists.

summaries.title: "Semi-Local" / Compositional Codes
summaries.gist: Representing objects by composing independent features like color and shape needs far fewer neurons, generalizes across unseen combinations, and stays interpretable, though at the cost of losing superposition's storage efficiency.

summaries.title: "Dense" / Maximal Superposition Codes
summaries.gist: A dense superposed code can represent far more unrelated objects than it has neurons, but sacrifices linear probing of individual features and requires abandoning composition to make superposition possible.

summaries.title: Composition vs Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition compete for the same exponential encoding space, so a representation cannot maximize both generalization and feature storage at once.
summaries.question: composition versus superposition — why can't a network maximize both at once? (a volume argument)

summaries.title: Two Strategies, Not One Spectrum
summaries.gist: The four codes seem to lie on one continuous spectrum from local to distributed, but actually reflect two orthogonal strategies, composition and superposition, that Thorpe's mixed "semi-distributed" example combines.

summaries.title: The Trade-off Formalized
summaries.gist: With a fixed number of encoding bits, fully composable features require exponential space and thus limit storage, while non-composing features can be packed into that same exponential volume via superposition.

summaries.title: Mixing Composition and Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition can partially coexist because sparse, rarely-combined features leave "holes" in compositional space that can store other features in superposition.
summaries.question: composition and superposition — how can sparse features let both coexist? (a mechanism)

summaries.title: Sparsity Enables Superposition
summaries.gist: When features are dense, networks can represent only one feature per neuron, but when combinations are sparse, the low-probability gaps in compositional space can be repurposed to store extra features in superposition.

summaries.title: Semi-Distributed Code Example
summaries.gist: Thorpe's "semi-distributed" code composes color and shape features while placing each set in mutual superposition, so its units are better seen as directions—combinations of neurons—representing features, not single meanings.

summaries.title: Conclusion
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition are distinct, competing notions of distributed representation whose properties differ, and understanding this structure is essential for reverse engineering neural networks.
summaries.question: composition and superposition — why does distinguishing them matter for understanding networks? (a recommendation)

summaries.title: Two Competing Notions
summaries.gist: "Distributed representations" actually names two different, sometimes mixable but fundamentally competing ideas—composition and superposition—and treating them as one blurs their very different properties.

summaries.title: Why Composition Matters for Understanding
summaries.gist: Composition lets researchers understand neural network representations using a linear number of independent features instead of an exponential amount of underlying volume, which is critical for genuinely understanding networks.

glossary.name: Superposition
glossary.senseHere: Packing more features into a layer than it has neurons, by letting each neuron respond to several unrelated features at once. Retrieving any one feature back out requires a nonlinearity, and most features can't be picked out by a simple linear probe.

glossary.name: distributed representation
glossary.senseHere: A representation where information is spread across many neurons firing together rather than one neuron per item. The piece argues this label actually hides two different, competing strategies: composition and superposition.

glossary.name: Composition
glossary.senseHere: Building a representation of a complex stimulus by combining separate, independent feature directions, like a color feature and a shape feature adding together to represent a colored shape. It lets a small number of features generate an exponentially larger number of representable combinations, and each component stays linearly readable.

glossary.name: local code
glossary.senseHere: A scheme with one dedicated neuron for each distinct stimulus (e.g. a separate neuron for every color-shape pair), so only one neuron fires per item and none of them shares meaning across items.

glossary.name: Thorpe (1989)
glossary.background: A neuroscience paper by Simon Thorpe that laid out example neural codes — local, semi-local, semi-distributed, and highly-distributed — to illustrate the spectrum between 'local' and 'distributed' coding in the brain. Olah borrows Thorpe's shape/color examples wholesale and reinterprets them through the composition/superposition distinction.

glossary.name: linear probe
glossary.senseHere: A simple linear readout trained to detect whether some property (like 'red') is present in a layer's activity. The piece notes such a probe can succeed even when the underlying code has no genuine single feature for that property, so probe success alone can't prove a feature is really represented.
